title: Blockers and the Shape of a Shift
endLine: How a blocker shifts or lowers curves across doses reveals its mechanism.

scenes.tts: A receptor reserve lets a tissue respond fully with mostly empty receptors. Naloxone can reverse a morphine overdose within minutes without reacting with morphine. How does a blocker's curve shift reveal its mechanism?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's 16:9 world and colour map without resetting. The row of twenty BLUE receptors sits on a GREY membrane above the GREEN response bar, starting at 100% response with one receptor occupied (carrying over the 5% reserve frame), alongside the GREEN log-dose response curve. Keep 'schematic' at lower right on the receptor strip. Introduce GOLD blocker tokens labelled 'naloxone' drifting beside GREEN agonist tokens labelled 'morphine'; the two never touch in solution. As GOLD tokens enter BLUE pockets, the GREEN response bar falls, the baseline curve ghosts to GREY, and a large question mark rises over the graph. No molecular structure is drawn.
scenes.narration: A receptor reserve lets a tissue respond fully with mostly empty receptors. Naloxone can reverse a morphine overdose within minutes without reacting with morphine. How does a blocker's curve shift reveal its mechanism?

scenes.visual: Over the carried membrane and curve world, display the title 'Blockers and the Shape of a Shift' for two seconds. GREEN agonist and GOLD blocker tokens drift gently above the twenty BLUE receptors without touching each other, while the question mark over the graph breathes softly.

scenes.tts: Start with a competitive antagonist, like naloxone. It binds reversibly at the agonist's own site and switches nothing on. One receptor holds agonist or blocker, never both. Add enough agonist, and it wins the sites back.
scenes.visual: Zoom into six BLUE receptors on the GREY membrane so they fill 65% of the frame height, keeping the GREEN response bar directly below. GOLD tokens labelled 'competitive blocker' slip into BLUE pockets and unbind repeatedly; GOLD-occupied pockets stay dark with no arrow to the bar. A GREEN token labelled 'agonist' bounces off a GOLD-occupied pocket, then enters as GOLD releases and lights the bar. Flood the space above with many GREEN tokens until they crowd GOLD out and refill the GREEN bar to 100%. Keep labels to 'receptor', 'agonist', 'competitive blocker', 'same site', and 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Start with a competitive antagonist, like naloxone. It binds reversibly at the agonist's own site and switches nothing on. One receptor holds agonist or blocker, never both. Add enough agonist, and it wins the sites back.

scenes.tts: On a log dose axis, each step multiplies the dose by ten. The curve slides right in parallel: at every response level, the dose needed rises by the same factor. That factor is the dose ratio. Enough agonist still reaches the full ceiling, so this block is surmountable.
scenes.visual: Expand the log-dose response graph to fill 65% of the frame, keeping a compact strip of BLUE receptors above. Retain the GREY ghost of the unblocked curve. Compute and draw a GOLD competitive curve shifted right in parallel by a dose ratio of 11 (1.04 log units), reaching the exact same 100% ceiling. Draw a horizontal dashed guide at 50% response linking the GREY baseline curve to the GOLD curve, and span the gap with a bracket labelled 'dose ratio'. Keep labels concise: 'parallel shift', 'same maximum', 'dose ratio'.
scenes.narration: On a log dose axis, each step multiplies the dose by ten. The curve slides right in parallel: at every response level, the dose needed rises by the same factor. That factor is the dose ratio. Enough agonist still reaches the full ceiling, so this block is surmountable.

scenes.tts: Other blockers are insurmountable: more agonist cannot overcome them. A non-competitive blocker binds elsewhere on the receptor, or stops a downstream step. Even with every agonist site filled, the response hits a lower ceiling. An irreversible blocker bonds covalently to the agonist site, so it cannot be washed off or outcompeted.
scenes.visual: Keep the same receptor strip and graph layout. First introduce PURPLE tokens labelled 'non-competitive blocker' latching onto side pockets of the BLUE receptors and clamping the downstream GREEN gauge; even as GREEN agonist fills the main pockets, the gauge caps low and a schematic PURPLE curve flattens well below 100% ('lower maximum'). Then replace PURPLE with the first film's RED tokens labelled 'irreversible blocker', locking onto the BLUE main pockets with a lock badge ('covalent bond'). Keep 'schematic' at lower right.
scenes.narration: Other blockers are insurmountable: more agonist cannot overcome them. A non-competitive blocker binds elsewhere on the receptor, or stops a downstream step. Even with every agonist site filled, the response hits a lower ceiling. An irreversible blocker bonds covalently to the agonist site, so it cannot be washed off or outcompeted.

scenes.tts: Now test an unknown blocker at one concentration. The agonist curve slides right in parallel, with the same maximum. Does that single curve prove the blocker is a reversible competitive antagonist?
scenes.visual: Keep the carried graph and receptor strip. Show the GREY baseline curve and one WHITE unknown-blocker curve shifted right in parallel (computed at a 2-fold shift, consistent with both simple competition at one reference dose and 50% receptor removal under the first film's 5% reserve model), reaching the exact same 100% ceiling. Above the membrane, WHITE tokens hover ambiguously without showing release or covalent locking. Place the question 'One parallel shift = competitive blocker?' across the top with an empty choice marker.
scenes.narration: Now test an unknown blocker at one concentration. The agonist curve slides right in parallel, with the same maximum. Does that single curve prove the blocker is a reversible competitive antagonist?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the question 'One parallel shift = competitive blocker?' and the single shifted WHITE curve at 100% maximum visible. WHITE tokens drift gently above the BLUE receptors and the empty choice marker pulses softly. Do not shift the curve or reveal an answer.

scenes.tts: No. With a receptor reserve, a small irreversible dose also slides the curve right before the ceiling drops. Only higher doses separate them. To name the mechanism, watch how rising doses reshape the agonist curve.
scenes.visual: Replace the choice marker with 'Not from one dose'. Split the single WHITE curve into two diverging rising-dose families on the same axes. In GOLD, a competitive blocker keeps sliding right at 100% maximum (computed dose ratios 2, 11, and 101). In RED, the first film's irreversible blocker (computed from the lesson's sharp 5% reserve model: 50% removed gives Kd/19 at 100%; 90% removed gives Kd/3 at 100%; more than 95% removed collapses the ceiling) matches the early shift, then drops below 100%. Label 'competitive: same ceiling' and 'irreversible: ceiling drops'.
scenes.narration: No. With a receptor reserve, a small irreversible dose also slides the curve right before the ceiling drops. Only higher doses separate them. To name the mechanism, watch how rising doses reshape the agonist curve.

scenes.tts: Heinz Schild made rising blocker doses a test for competition. Raise the blocker tenfold, twice. Simple competition at equilibrium might give dose ratios of two, eleven and one hundred one. Subtract one, since no blocker means a ratio of one. That leaves one, ten and one hundred. As logs against log blocker dose, they form a straight line of slope one.
scenes.caption: Heinz Schild made rising blocker doses a test for competition. Raise the blocker tenfold, twice. Simple competition at equilibrium might give dose ratios of 2, 11 and 101. Subtract 1, since no blocker means a ratio of 1. That leaves 1, 10 and 100. As logs against log blocker dose, they form a straight line of slope 1.
scenes.visual: Slide the GOLD family of competitive curves (computed dose ratios 2, 11, and 101 at tenfold-spaced blocker concentrations) into the left third of the frame. On the right two thirds, build a computed Schild plot with y-axis 'log(dose ratio - 1)' and x-axis 'log [blocker]'. Morph the three horizontal dose-ratio brackets into three GOLD points at relative log coordinates (0, 0), (1, 1), and (2, 2), each labelled with its numbers as spoken ('2 − 1 = 1', '11 − 1 = 10', '101 − 1 = 100'), and connect them with a straight GOLD line carrying a rise-over-run triangle labelled 'slope = 1'.
scenes.narration: Heinz Schild made rising blocker doses a test for competition. Raise the blocker tenfold, twice. Simple competition at equilibrium might give dose ratios of 2, 11 and 101. Subtract 1, since no blocker means a ratio of 1. That leaves 1, 10 and 100. As logs against log blocker dose, they form a straight line of slope 1.

scenes.tts: A different slope, or a curve, warns that an assumption failed. Equilibrium may not hold, or the tissue may remove agonist. A blocker binding elsewhere, or a second receptor, can bend it too. Even slope one over a narrow range does not rule those out.
scenes.caption: A different slope, or a curve, warns that an assumption failed. Equilibrium may not hold, or the tissue may remove agonist. A blocker binding elsewhere, or a second receptor, can bend it too. Even slope 1 over a narrow range does not rule those out.
scenes.visual: Keep the Schild plot centred with the straight GOLD slope-1 line dimmed as a reference. Overlay two schematic RED/PURPLE alternatives: a flatter tilted line labelled 'slope not 1' and a bending curve labelled 'curves at high dose'. Around the edge, display four compact warning badges one by one (at most 5 words each): 'not at equilibrium', 'agonist removed', 'binds elsewhere', 'second receptor'. Then bracket a tiny segment where the curving line briefly hugs the slope-1 line and label it 'narrow range: inconclusive'. Keep 'schematic' at lower right.
scenes.narration: A different slope, or a curve, warns that an assumption failed. Equilibrium may not hold, or the tissue may remove agonist. A blocker binding elsewhere, or a second receptor, can bend it too. Even slope 1 over a narrow range does not rule those out.

scenes.tts: Return to naloxone and morphine. In a simple preparation at equilibrium, naloxone fills morphine's receptor without activating it, shifting morphine's curve right. That reduces the signalling behind an overdose's slowed breathing, without touching morphine. Yet clinical reversal depends on time, and equilibrium ratios alone do not predict it.
scenes.visual: Transform the Schild plot back into the carried twenty BLUE receptors (labelled 'mu-opioid receptor') on the GREY membrane beside the log-dose response graph. GREEN morphine tokens occupy pockets and drive the GREEN response bar; GOLD naloxone tokens compete them off without contacting them in solution, sliding the morphine curve right in parallel (schematic) while the signalling bar drops. Then bring in a gently ticking clock badge labelled 'clinical reversal: time-dependent' beside a dimmed 'equilibrium ratio' tag to mark where the simple equilibrium picture stops. Keep 'schematic' at lower right.
scenes.narration: Return to naloxone and morphine. In a simple preparation at equilibrium, naloxone fills morphine's receptor without activating it, shifting morphine's curve right. That reduces the signalling behind an overdose's slowed breathing, without touching morphine. Yet clinical reversal depends on time, and equilibrium ratios alone do not predict it.

scenes.tts: Across rising doses, a curve's shift and ceiling separate surmountable competition from insurmountable block. Next: can two curves in an unknown tissue measure a blocker's grip?
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full carried world: the twenty BLUE receptors above, with the GOLD parallel competitive curves at 100%, the RED irreversible curve dropping after its reserve, and the faint slope-1 Schild line beside them. Cover the downstream pathway gauge with a frosted box labelled 'unknown amplifier' next to two parallel shifted curves and an unanswered question mark, without answering the text's prediction on measuring antagonist affinity.
scenes.narration: Across rising doses, a curve's shift and ceiling separate surmountable competition from insurmountable block. Next: can two curves in an unknown tissue measure a blocker's grip?

scenes.visual: End card with one line only: 'How a blocker shifts or lowers curves across doses reveals its mechanism.' Set it large and centred on the dark background. No title, logo, URL, subtitle or smaller line appears. Behind the text, faint GOLD parallel shifted curves and a faint RED lowered curve breathe gently at low contrast.
